title: Why Do You Sound Better Singing in the Shower?

lines.text: In the shower, hard tiles reflect your voice back at you.
The reflections overlap, making a short tail of sound called reverb.
That can make your voice sound fuller and last longer.
Now swap the tiles for towels and curtains.
They absorb more sound, so less bounces back.
My bathroom has more talent than me.

demonstration.description: One original Kai vocal take, copied unchanged for both comparisons. Add a local room impulse response only to the wet version.
demonstration.captionPolicy: No invented lexical captions over the nonverbal sung demo; room labels and visible vocal action carry the comparison.

story: Open mid-performance on the wet sung vocal; a short push and live sound arcs establish action immediately.
Play the wet vocal, then cut the room effect away and replay the identical dry source. Miko reacts.
The two waveforms align to establish the shared recording.
Follow pulses from the singer to the tiled walls and back, highlighting each contact.
Keep reflected pulses visible after the direct sound ends; a short waveform tail remains.
Tile panels morph into fabric surfaces; arriving pulses shrink and fade into the material.
Compare both rooms with the same source. Resolve on Miko's deadpan bathroom line.
Return to the opening room and confident pose during the final sound tail.
